title: Idioms and design patterns
intro: An idiom is the way Rust code usually says a common thing: wrap a number in a type of its own, build a value in one place that checks it, make a wrong state impossible to write. Many are design patterns you already know, trimmed because enums, traits and ownership do part of the work. This page shows the ones you will read most, the compiler error each one turns a mistake into, and the habits that look like idioms and are not.

coming_from.go: A defined type (`type UserID int`) is the newtype, and functional options are the cousin of the Rust builder. Go chose the zero value on purpose (`var p Port` is `0`), and most Go types are designed so it is valid; the cost shows when it should not be, so "a `Port` that cannot be invalid" is a convention there. A Rust type has no zero value unless you write one, so a `Port` comes from the function you wrote. Cleanup is also different: `defer` runs at the end of the function, a Rust `Drop` guard at the end of its scope.
coming_from.kotlin: `value class` is the newtype, default and named arguments plus `copy` do much of what a Rust builder or `..Default::default()` does, and a `sealed` hierarchy is an enum. Rust has no named or default arguments, so the builder is more common than in Kotlin. `use {}` is the nearest to a `Drop` guard, but it is written by the caller at each use; a Rust guard runs without it.
coming_from.python: The same designs exist, checked by the compiler where Python relies on convention. `typing.NewType` is erased at run time (the page below passes an order id to a function that wants a user id, and it runs). A class that checks in `__init__` or `__post_init__` is the nearest Python form of "parse, don't validate": no invalid `Port` gets built, but the failure is an exception, so nothing makes the caller handle it. A `with` block is the nearest to a `Drop` guard, but the caller has to write it.
coming_from.typescript: Branded types and discriminated unions are your newtype and enum, and `tsc --strict` checks them. They are erased when the program runs (the page below prints `typeof` of a branded id: `number`). A Rust newtype takes no more space than its field, so it is gone at run time too; what differs is the build, where no cast turns a number into a `Port`.
coming_from.java: A `record` around one field is the newtype, a nested `Builder` class is the builder, and `sealed` interfaces with a `switch` are enums. A Strategy is already an interface or a lambda in Java, and a Rust trait or closure is the same thing; State has no base class to subclass per state, so it is an enum or a typestate. `try`-with-resources is the nearest to `Drop`, but you can forget to write the `try`.
coming_from.csharp: A `readonly record struct` is the newtype, `init` properties with `with` expressions do the job of a builder and `..Default::default()`, and `using` is the nearest to a `Drop` guard. A Rust type has no constructors: an associated function such as `new` or `parse` is an ordinary function that returns the value, so it can return a `Result`.
coming_from.c: `typedef int UserId;` names a type without making one: the page below passes an order id to a function that wants a user id, and it compiles under `-Wall -Wextra`. A one-field Rust struct is a new type. Designated initializers (`{.port = 9000}`) give C zero for everything you leave out, and cleanup is `goto cleanup` by hand, where Rust runs `Drop` for you.
coming_from.cpp: RAII is where `Drop` comes from, an `explicit` one-field struct is the newtype, and `std::variant` is an enum. What changes is that a Rust function builds the value, so it can return a `Result` the caller has to handle (a C++ constructor has no return value, so it throws), and a moved-from value cannot be used.

notes: A newtype is a struct with one field. It is a different type from the field's type, so the compiler refuses to mix them up, and its field can be private so that your own functions build it.
"Parse, don't validate": turn loosely typed input into a type that cannot be invalid, once, at the edge; everything after takes the strong type.

Enums with data make illegal states unrepresentable: a download that is both done and failed has no spelling. A typestate goes further and puts the state in the type, so calling `send` before `connect` is a compile error.
`Default` with `..Default::default()` and a builder stand in for the named and default arguments that Rust does not have. A guard type with a `Drop` impl ties cleanup to a scope.

Some habits look like idioms and are not: a `.clone()` that silences the borrow checker, `unwrap()` in a library, `Rc<RefCell<_>>` for everything, text where an enum belongs, generics nobody uses, and `Box<dyn Error>` as a library's error type. Each has a before and an after below.

gotcha.title: Copying a struct with `..` and then using the original
gotcha.looks_fine: Copying a struct and changing one field leaves the original alone and usable: `copy(port = 9000)` in Kotlin, `replace` in Python, `{...base}` in TypeScript, `with` in C#, `test := base` in Go.
gotcha.rust_sees: `..base` takes the fields you did not name: `name` and `verbose`. `verbose` is `Copy`, so it is copied, but `name` is a `String`, so it is moved into `test`. `base` is now partly moved, and printing all of it is an error.
gotcha.why: A `String` has one owner, and a copy that allocates is something Rust makes you ask for with `.clone()`. So `..base` moves what it cannot copy, and `base` stays whole when the fields taken were all `Copy` (name the `String` yourself and it works; [Structs](/learn/structs/) shows the same rule). The fix is `..base.clone()` when you want a full copy, or `..Default::default()` when you only wanted defaults.

go.says: Go runs this and prints both structs. `test := base` copies the three fields. The string is shared, which is fine because a Go string cannot change.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints both. `copy(port = 9000)` makes a new `Config`; the `String` is immutable, so the two share it.
kotlin.code:
data class Config(val name: String, val port: Int, val verbose: Boolean)

fun main() {
    val base = Config("service", 8080, false)
    val test = base.copy(port = 9000)
    println(base)
    println(test)
}
kotlin.out:
Config(name=service, port=8080, verbose=false)
Config(name=service, port=9000, verbose=false)

python.says: Python runs this and prints both. `dataclasses.replace` builds a new `Config`; the `str` is immutable, so the two share it.
python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass
class Config:
    name: str
    port: int
    verbose: bool


base = Config("service", 8080, False)
test = replace(base, port=9000)
print(base)
print(test)
python.out:
Config(name='service', port=8080, verbose=False)
Config(name='service', port=9000, verbose=False)

typescript.says: TypeScript runs this and prints both. The spread copies the properties one level deep; the string is a primitive. An object-valued property would be shared by both.
typescript.out:
{ name: 'service', port: 8080, verbose: false }
{ name: 'service', port: 9000, verbose: false }

java.says: Java runs this and prints both. A record has no copy-with, so you pass the fields you keep by hand; the `String` is immutable and shared.
java.out:
Config[name=service, port=8080, verbose=false]
Config[name=service, port=9000, verbose=false]

csharp.says: C# runs this and prints both. `with` copies the record and changes `Port`; the `string` is immutable and shared.
csharp.out:
Config { Name = service, Port = 8080, Verbose = False }
Config { Name = service, Port = 9000, Verbose = False }

c.says: C runs this and prints both. The struct assignment copies the fields, and here `name` is a pointer to a string literal that both copies share. With a `malloc`ed name, freeing both copies would free it twice (not run).

cpp.says: C++ runs this and prints both. The copy duplicates the `std::string` too, so both are whole; the allocation is the cost Rust asks you to write as `.clone()`.
